title: Microsoft Translator adds Inuktitut (2021), Inuinnaqtun and romanized Inuktitut (2022) and Inuktitut text-to-speech (2024) with the Government of Nunavut
summary: Neural MT for Inuktut dialects built with the Government of Nunavut and volunteer speakers; Nunatsiaq News and VICE report launches and translation errors; no measured user outcome documented.
account: Microsoft added Inuktitut text translation to Microsoft Translator, Office and Translator for Bing on 27 January 2021 (Arctic Portal, relaying the Microsoft Translator blog; date used here), after working with the Government of Nunavut for language data, with Inuktitut speakers volunteering to validate and test translations. VICE (18 February 2021) reported Nunavut language officials finding the output “riddled with mistakes” (Solomon Awa: “Sometimes it's close, but sometimes it gave the opposite meaning, or one that was misleading”) while languages commissioner Karliin Aariak called it “a great tool to be like a first step” and retired Université Laval researcher Louis-Jacques Dorais called it a “tour de force” despite a wrong test sentence. Nunatsiaq News (28 February 2022) reported that Inuinnaqtun and romanized Inuktitut were added during Uqausirmut Quviasuutiqarniq, with fewer than 600 fluent Inuinnaqtun speakers per the Kitikmeot Heritage Society; Microsoft's own feature (1 February 2022) says “Text translation is based on neural machine translation models”, that the Government of Nunavut “turned to the community to help build and test the language models”, and lists intended uses (unilingual patients communicating with doctors, younger people with elders, emails in Office) without data. Nunatsiaq News (9 December 2024) reported the 5 December launch of Inuktitut text-to-speech voices “Taqqiq” and “Siqiniq”, built from thousands of government documents, hired speakers' recordings and Bible Society and Nunavut Inuit Heritage Trust audio, noting presenters' accounts of the translator confusing “condo and condom, and prime rib and prime minister”; voice contributor Leah Ayaruaq McKay said she plans to use it to help her husband learn Inuktitut. Government of Nunavut web pages were behind a bot check and no Wayback capture existed. No source on file measures use, accuracy or an outcome for any user.
purpose: Built to translate text between Inuktut dialects and other languages (and, from 2024, to read Inuktitut aloud) so that residents, learners and government users can read and write in Inuktut; the launches are that intended use.
system: Microsoft Translator Inuktitut, Inuinnaqtun and romanized Inuktitut text translation (neural machine translation) and Inuktitut text-to-speech
developer: Microsoft (Azure Cognitive Services Translator and Speech) with the Government of Nunavut and community volunteers, including the Kitikmeot Heritage Society for Inuinnaqtun
deployer: Government of Nunavut; public users of Microsoft Translator, Office and Bing
segment: Public translation tools for Inuktut dialects
taxonomy_note: Loose fit; the good is an Indigenous official language made usable in mainstream software, with no measured outcome and reported translation errors.

ratings.reason: Users are described (a translator who found errors, a voice contributor planning to use it for her husband's learning); no measured benefit for any person is documented.
The Government of Nunavut's and Microsoft's stated uses (healthcare communication, Office email, compliance with language law) are expectations without reported data.
Language-vitality effects are asserted by officials; VICE notes Inuktut use fell from 72 to 65 percent between 2001 and 2016, without any link to the tool.

ai_role.statement: Microsoft states the translation is neural machine translation trained on Government of Nunavut data and validated by volunteer speakers. Independent reporting records both the launches and specific wrong translations (opposite meanings in 2021; “condo and condom” confusions recounted in 2024), and translators said the output needs a fluent reviewer. No source on file reports a user outcome, usage figure or accuracy measurement, so what the system contributed beyond availability is undocumented.

headline: Microsoft Translator adds Inuktitut and Inuinnaqtun with Nunavut

later.note: After the January 2021 launch, Inuinnaqtun and romanized Inuktitut were added in February 2022 and Inuktitut text-to-speech voices launched on 5 December 2024, while presenters still reported word confusions.
later.quote: Microsoft Canada and the Government of Nunavut announced Dec. 5 that Inuktitut text-to-speech is available now on Microsoft Translator.

claim_basis: Four independent news reports and the makers' press release are on file. There is no independent study or report and no finding by a regulator or court.
